title: Your First SELECT
schema: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT NOT NULL, score INTEGER NOT NULL)
task: Return the name of every student from the students table. Return just the name column. Any row order is accepted; keep repeated names.
referenceQuery: SELECT name FROM students
explanation: SELECT chooses the column you want to see. FROM names the table. SELECT name FROM students returns one name for each student.
hint: Choose just the name column. You do not need a filter.

title: Pick Two Columns
schema: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT NOT NULL, score INTEGER NOT NULL)
task: Return every student’s name and city from students, in that column order. Any row order is accepted.
referenceQuery: SELECT name, city FROM students
explanation: Separate column names with a comma: SELECT name, city. You do not need to return id or score.
hint: Put the two requested column names after SELECT, separated by a comma.

title: Students in Chennai
schema: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT NOT NULL, score INTEGER NOT NULL)
task: Return only the names of students whose city is 'Chennai'. Any row order is accepted.
referenceQuery: SELECT name FROM students WHERE city = 'Chennai'
explanation: WHERE keeps rows that match a condition. Put text values such as 'Chennai' inside single quotes.
hint: Filter the city column with WHERE. Text values need single quotes.

title: Who Passed?
schema: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT NOT NULL, score INTEGER NOT NULL)
task: A student passes with a score of 50 or more. Return the name and score of every passing student, in that column order. A score of exactly 50 counts as a pass. Any row order is accepted.
referenceQuery: SELECT name, score FROM students WHERE score >= 50
explanation: Use >= to mean greater than or equal to. WHERE score >= 50 includes students scoring exactly 50.
hint: Use a greater-than-or-equal comparison so a score of exactly 50 passes.

title: Under 100
schema: CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, price INTEGER NOT NULL, stock INTEGER NOT NULL)
task: Return the name and price of products costing less than 100, in that column order. Products priced exactly 100 do not qualify. Any row order is accepted.
referenceQuery: SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price < 100
explanation: Use < for a strict less-than comparison. WHERE price < 100 excludes a price of exactly 100.
hint: Use a strict less-than comparison on price.

title: Ready to Sell
schema: CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, price INTEGER NOT NULL, stock INTEGER NOT NULL)
task: Return the names of products with stock greater than 0. Stock means the number of units available. Any row order is accepted.
referenceQuery: SELECT name FROM products WHERE stock > 0
explanation: WHERE stock > 0 keeps only products with at least one unit available.
hint: Filter stock, not price. Zero units means the product is unavailable.

title: A to Z
schema: CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, price INTEGER NOT NULL, stock INTEGER NOT NULL)
task: Return every product name sorted alphabetically from A to Z. Return only the name column and keep repeated names.
referenceQuery: SELECT name FROM products ORDER BY name ASC
explanation: ORDER BY name ASC sorts names in ascending order. ASC is the default, so ORDER BY name also works.
hint: ORDER BY can sort a text column. Ascending order means A to Z.

title: One of Each City
schema: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT NOT NULL, score INTEGER NOT NULL)
task: Return the city column from students, showing each city only once. Any row order is accepted.
referenceQuery: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM students
explanation: DISTINCT removes repeated values from the result. Several students can share a city, but it should appear only once here.
hint: DISTINCT removes duplicate values from a selected column.

title: Just Three Rows
schema: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT NOT NULL, score INTEGER NOT NULL)
task: Return the id and name of the first 3 students by smallest id, in that column order. Sort by id ascending. If fewer than 3 students exist, return all of them.
referenceQuery: SELECT id, name FROM students ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT 3
explanation: ORDER BY id puts the smallest ids first. LIMIT 3 keeps at most three rows; it does not add rows to a smaller table.
hint: Sort by id before limiting the number of returned rows. IDs may have gaps.

title: How Many Students?
schema: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT NOT NULL, score INTEGER NOT NULL)
task: Return one number: the total number of students. Count every row, even if two students share a name. An empty table should return 0.
referenceQuery: SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM students
explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows. It produces a single total, and returns 0 when there are no students.
hint: COUNT(*) counts every row, including students who share a name.

title: Add Up the Stock
schema: CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, price INTEGER NOT NULL, stock INTEGER NOT NULL)
task: Return one number: the sum of the stock column across all products. Count units, not product rows. If the table is empty, return one row containing NULL, which is what SUM returns by default.
referenceQuery: SELECT SUM(stock) AS total FROM products
explanation: SUM(stock) adds all the stock values together. The sample is 12 + 0 + 8 + 5 + 0 = 25. SUM returns NULL for an empty table.
hint: Use SUM on the stock column. Counting rows counts products, not units.

title: The Highest Score
schema: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT NOT NULL, score INTEGER NOT NULL)
task: Return one number: the highest score in students. Return just the score, not a student name. If the table is empty, return one row containing NULL, which is what MAX returns by default.
referenceQuery: SELECT MAX(score) AS highest FROM students
explanation: MAX(score) finds the largest value in that column. It returns one value even if several students share the highest score, and NULL for an empty table.
hint: MAX finds the largest value in a column without needing to sort.

title: Above Department Average
schema: CREATE TABLE departments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)
CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept_id INTEGER, salary INTEGER, hired TEXT)
task: List the names of employees who earn more than the average salary of their own department.
referenceQuery:
SELECT e.name FROM employees e
    JOIN (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) a FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id) d
      ON e.dept_id=d.dept_id WHERE e.salary>d.a
hiddenDatasets: UPDATE employees SET salary=salary*2+17, name='New_' || id
explanation: Compute the average per department, then compare each employee against their own group. A company-wide average answers a different question.
hint: Calculate a separate average for each department, then compare employees only to their own department.

title: Department Headcount
schema: CREATE TABLE departments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)
CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept_id INTEGER, salary INTEGER, hired TEXT)
task: For each department, return its name and the number of employees. Order by department name.
referenceQuery:
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.id) AS headcount FROM departments d
    LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id=d.id GROUP BY d.id,d.name ORDER BY d.name
hiddenDatasets: UPDATE employees SET salary=salary*2+17, name='New_' || id
explanation: Start with departments and LEFT JOIN employees. COUNT(e.id) counts real employees; COUNT(*) counts the empty department row too.
hint: Start from departments and use a LEFT JOIN so empty departments stay in the result. Count employee IDs.

title: Top Earner Per Department
schema: CREATE TABLE departments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)
CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept_id INTEGER, salary INTEGER, hired TEXT)
task: Return department id, employee name, and salary for every highest-paid employee in each department. Include ties. Order by department id, then employee name.
referenceQuery:
SELECT d.id, e.name, e.salary FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.id=e.dept_id
    WHERE e.salary=(SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees x WHERE x.dept_id=e.dept_id)
    ORDER BY d.id , e.name
hiddenDatasets: UPDATE employees SET salary=salary*2+17, name='New_' || id
explanation: Use a correlated MAX or RANK partitioned by department. Include every employee tied for the highest salary.
hint: Compare each salary with the maximum for its department. More than one employee can tie for first.

title: Second Highest Salary
schema: CREATE TABLE departments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)
CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept_id INTEGER, salary INTEGER, hired TEXT)
task: Return the second highest distinct salary across all employees. Return no rows if there are fewer than two distinct salaries.
referenceQuery: SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
hiddenDatasets: UPDATE employees SET salary=salary*2+17, name='New_' || id
explanation: Remove duplicate salaries before finding the second value. Return no rows if fewer than two distinct salaries exist.
hint: Remove duplicate salaries before skipping the largest one.

title: Empty Departments
schema: CREATE TABLE departments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)
CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept_id INTEGER, salary INTEGER, hired TEXT)
task: Return the names of departments that have no employees.
referenceQuery: SELECT d.name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id=d.id WHERE e.id IS NULL
hiddenDatasets: UPDATE employees SET salary=salary*2+17, name='New_' || id
explanation: A LEFT JOIN with a NULL employee id, or NOT EXISTS, preserves departments with no employees.
hint: Use NOT EXISTS or a LEFT JOIN to find departments without a matching employee.

title: Customer Order Totals
schema: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER, placed TEXT)
task: Return each customer's name and their total order amount, highest total first. Only customers with at least one order. Break total ties by customer id ascending. Customers with the same name are separate customers.
referenceQuery:
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
    GROUP BY c.id,c.name ORDER BY total DESC, c.id
hiddenDatasets: UPDATE customers SET name='New_' || id, city='Region_' || city
explanation: Join customers to orders, group by customer identity, and sum amounts. Different customers may share a name.
hint: Join customers to orders and group by customer ID before summing. Names are not unique.

title: Customers Without Orders
schema: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER, placed TEXT)
task: Return the names of customers who have never placed an order.
referenceQuery: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
hiddenDatasets: UPDATE customers SET name='New_' || id, city='Region_' || city
explanation: NOT EXISTS handles unmatched customers even when an order has a NULL customer_id. NOT IN with NULL behaves differently.
hint: Look for customers without a matching order. NOT EXISTS works even if an order has no customer ID.

title: Average Order Value By City
schema: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER, placed TEXT)
task: For each city, return the city and the average order amount rounded to 2 decimals, for cities that have orders. Order by city.
referenceQuery:
SELECT c.city, ROUND(AVG(o.amount),2) AS avg_amount FROM customers c
    JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id GROUP BY c.city ORDER BY c.city
hiddenDatasets: UPDATE customers SET name='New_' || id, city='Region_' || city
explanation: Average the order rows within each city, not the per-customer averages. Round only the final result.
hint: Average the individual order amounts within each city, then round the result.

title: Repeat Customers
schema: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER, placed TEXT)
task: Return the names of customers who placed more than 2 orders.
referenceQuery:
SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
    GROUP BY c.id,c.name HAVING COUNT(o.id)>2
hiddenDatasets: UPDATE customers SET name='New_' || id, city='Region_' || city
explanation: Group by customer identity and use HAVING COUNT(*) > 2. Customers with exactly two orders must be excluded.
hint: Count orders per customer and filter groups with HAVING.

title: Running Order Total
schema: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER, placed TEXT)
task: For customer id 1, return each order id, amount, and running total. Order by placed date, then order id. Include each order individually when dates tie.
referenceQuery: SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY placed, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running FROM orders WHERE customer_id=1 ORDER BY placed, id
hiddenDatasets: UPDATE customers SET name='New_' || id, city='Region_' || city
explanation: Use SUM(amount) OVER with ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING. Order by placed and id so same-day orders have a deterministic sequence.
hint: Use a SUM window ordered by placed and id. A ROWS frame handles orders on the same date separately.

title: Monthly Revenue
schema: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER, placed TEXT)
task: Return each month (YYYY-MM) and total revenue for that month, ordered by month.
referenceQuery:
SELECT substr(placed,1,7) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders
    GROUP BY month ORDER BY month
hiddenDatasets: UPDATE customers SET name='New_' || id, city='Region_' || city
explanation: Group using both year and month. Grouping only by month number combines different years.
hint: Group by both year and month together. SQLite substr can take the YYYY-MM part of a date.

title: Orders Above Overall Average
schema: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, city TEXT)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER, placed TEXT)
task: Return the ids of orders whose amount is greater than the overall average order amount.
referenceQuery: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders)
hiddenDatasets: UPDATE customers SET name='New_' || id, city='Region_' || city
explanation: Compare each amount to the average over all orders. Use a strict greater-than comparison.
hint: A scalar subquery can calculate the overall average for your WHERE comparison.
